1#main: Impurity of a kohen for a met mitzvah, for a nasi and teacher, and for which dead they mourn. In it are 11 seifim. It is a mitzvah to become impure for a met mitzvah — even a High Priest and a nazir going to slaughter his Pesach or circumcise his son, and he found a met mitzvah — behold he becomes impure for him.
2#main: He is not called met mitzvah for this purpose unless he found his head and majority; and if he found his head and majority except one limb — he returns to become impure for that limb.
3#main: What is met mitzvah? One found on the road or in a gentile city without grave-diggers, and from where he found him he cannot call an Israelite who will answer and come to attend to him and bury him — it is a mitzvah for him to move from there and not leave the dead, even to go to a city to bring grave-diggers; rather he becomes impure himself and buries him; but if Israelites were near the place of the dead so the finder calls them and they answer and come to bury him — this is not met mitzvah for the kohen to become impure for him; rather he calls them and they bury. If the townspeople came {Rama: (Ramban in Torat HaAdam and Rosh in laws of impurity)} — if he has all his needs, he withdraws his hand. {Rama: Some say if he finds none to bury him except for pay, he is not obligated to hire from his own — rather he becomes impure if he wishes (Nimmukei Yosef ch. HaIshah Rabba in the name of Ritva); a found dead person and we do not know whether gentile or Israelite — we follow the majority found there, if we cannot say every fixed case is half-and-half (Beit Yosef in the name of responsum of Rashba).}
4#main: All relatives for whom a kohen becomes impure — father, mother, son, daughter, brother and sister from his father who is a virgin, and his wife — mourn for them; and they added brother from mother and sister from mother, whether virgin or married, and married sister from father — who mourn for them even though a kohen does not become impure for them; and just as he mourns for his wife, so she mourns for him — specifically his fit married wife, but unfit or betrothed — not; but for his son, daughter, brother, and sister, even if unfit, he mourns — except his son, daughter, brother, and sister who are mamzer or from a gentile woman, for whom he does not mourn.
5#main: A convert who converted — he and his sons — or a freed slave — he and his mother — do not mourn for each other {Rama: (And the same if a convert converted with his mother — they do not mourn for them) (reasoning of the Rav from Mordechai laws of rejoicing from a case before R' Yitzchak, as we hold mourning on the first day is rabbinic).}
6#main: Whoever mourns for one — one mourns with him if one's relative died and specifically while before him; but if not before him, one need not practice mourning except for his wife — for even though he mourns for her, he does not mourn with her except for her father or mother because of honor for his father-in-law and mother-in-law; but for her brother, sister, or son or daughter from another man he does not mourn with her; nevertheless he cannot force her to adorn herself, but she may mix him a cup, spread his bed, and wash his face, hands, and feet; and likewise she does not mourn with him except when his father or mother died; but for his other relatives who died she does not mourn with him: {Rama: And some say that nowadays they are lenient in this mourning-with-the-mourner, for it is only because of honor for mourners, and now all practice to forgive; and so nowadays they do not mourn at all with mourners (Tur in the name of Rosh, and he in ch. Aveilut Met, and Ramban in Torat HaAdam and Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 1); and whoever is stringent in this is only among the astonished (Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 2); nevertheless they practice that all relatives disqualified for testimony for the dead show some mourning themselves all the first week — meaning until after the first Shabbat, when they do not bathe and somewhat change garments like other Shabbat (great ones of Austria practiced thus); and some places practice further stringency in other matters — the main point as I wrote; and all this is for close report or when he was at the death; but for distant report there is no place for this mourning at all (all explained in Torat HaAdam siman 291); one who wishes to be stringent for himself to mourn for one he need not, or wear black for his relative — they do not protest (Rosh klal 20).}
7#main: One does not mourn with relatives who mourn for their relative except when mourning the principal relative — such as son and brother mourning for son and daughter of theirs; but for relatives by marriage, such as son's wife died, or brother's wife, or daughter's husband, or sister's husband — he does not mourn for them.
8#main: A child — all thirty days, and day thirty included, they do not mourn for him even if his hair and nails were complete; from then on they mourn for him unless it is known he is eight months; and if it is clear his months were complete, such as one who married and separated and a live child was born at nine full months — even if he died the day he was born, they mourn for him {Rama: (doubt nine-month of the first or seven-month of the last — both mourn for him) (Mordechai laws of mourning and Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 1 and Beit Yosef in the name of Tosafot).}
9#main: Some say regarding twins that if one died within thirty days and the second lived and died after thirty days — they do not mourn for him.
10#main: For one's teacher from whom he learned wisdom — one practices laws of aninut except he blesses and leads grace, and mourns for him with shoe-removal and all laws of mourning one day: {Rama: (And Beit Yosef wrote in the name of R' Simchah that he must change his place in synagogue — however part of the day suffices).}
11#main: A nasi — even though all become impure for him, they do not mourn for him: {Rama: Some say they do not mourn for a firstborn son or bekhor who died to a person (Kol Bo and Rivash and Beit Yosef brought one who practiced thus and wrote it is an error); and the custom is an erroneous custom — rather they must mourn for them; nevertheless the custom spread in our city that father and mother do not follow their firstborn children to the cemetery; some say in time of plague they do not mourn {Rama: because of panic} (responsum of Maharil siman 50); and I heard some practiced thus.}
